english: After the First Emperor died, his lingering might shook regions of different customs.
Yet Chen She, son of a broken-window and rope-hinged door household, a hired bondsman and a banished conscript,
whose talents fell short of the ordinary man's, having neither the worth of Confucius or Mo Di nor the wealth of Tao Zhu or Yi Dun,
stepped forth from the ranks and rose from among the furrows, leading weary soldiers and commanding a few hundred men, wheeling about to attack Qin;
cutting wood for weapons, hoisting poles for banners, the world gathered like clouds and answered like echo, carrying grain to follow him as shadow follows form.
The bold champions east of the mountains thereupon rose together and destroyed the Qin clan.
Moreover, the world was not weak or small: the land of Yongzhou, the fastness of Xiao and Han, remained as before.
Chen She's station was no more exalted than the lords of Qi, Chu, Yan, Zhao, Han, Wei, Song, Wei and Zhongshan;
hoe handles and thorn shafts were no sharper than hooked halberds and long spears;
his band of banished conscripts was no match for the armies of the nine states;
in deep planning and far sight, in the arts of marching and employing troops, he could not match the men of former times.
Yet let the states east of the mountains have measured lengths and compared sizes with Chen She, weighed power and force—they would not be speakable of in the same breath.
Yet Qin, from a mere patch of ground, attained the might of ten thousand chariots, marshalled the eight provinces and made its fellow lords pay court, for more than a hundred years;
then it made the Six Directions its home and Xiao-Han its palace;
yet when one man rose in revolt the ancestral temples crumbled, its ruler died at another's hand, a laughing-stock to the world. Why?
In the sixteenth year of King Huiwen of Zhao, Lian Po led Zhao's army against Qi, crushed it, took Yangjin, and was appointed Chief Minister, his courage famed among the lords.
King Zhao of Qin heard of it and sent a letter to the King of Zhao, wishing to trade fifteen cities for the jade.
The King of Zhao consulted with General Lian Po and the great ministers: to give it, yet Qin's cities might never come, and they would be deceived in vain;
to refuse, and they feared Qin's armies would come.

My messenger said: 'I once attended Your Majesty at a meeting with the King of Yan on the border; the King of Yan privately grasped my hand, saying "I wish to be friends," and by this I knew it, so I wished to go.'
Xiangru told my messenger: 'Zhao is strong and Yan weak, and you enjoy the King of Zhao's favour, so the King of Yan wished to befriend you.'
Thereupon the king summoned Xiangru and asked: "The King of Qin offers fifteen cities for my jade—shall I give it?"
Xiangru said: "Qin asks the jade with cities, and if Zhao refuses, the fault lies with Zhao.
If Zhao gives the jade and Qin gives Zhao no cities, the fault lies with Qin.
Weighing the two courses, better to consent, and let the fault fall on Qin."
The king said: "Who could be sent?"
Xiangru said: "If Your Majesty has truly no one, I am willing to bear the jade and go as envoy."
"If the cities enter Zhao, the jade stays in Qin;
if not, I shall bring the jade back whole to Zhao."
The King of Zhao thereupon sent Xiangru bearing the jade westward into Qin.
